results.title: Bugs that broke driving - comma.ai blog
results.content: In October 2020 there were several complaints about openpilot crossing the inner laneline in turns. After looking at the examples they all appeared to happen in long sweeping turns at night, in all cases the driving model predictions for the path and lanelines that were biased towards the inside of the turn.

results.title: Anybody else find coding with AI "agents" incredibly frustrating? - Mac & iOS - Level1Techs Forums
results.content:
They are only good for solved problems. We get a co-pilot license at work, and it’s okay for small snippets. But any large generation it tries to predict always looks fucking awful. It’s difficult to read, and I’m always shocked if and when it actually works.

I haven’t done any machine learning since college (in undergrad we the Green Book. When I was in grad school, all the undergrads had the Blue Book. Kinda funny how you can tell when a CS major went to school by the color of the A.I. book).

But if you took A.I once in your life and are familiar with the basics of back propagation, 3Blue1Brown has a great video series on how LLMs work:

 explained visually | DL5") [...] # Anybody else find coding with AI "agents" incredibly frustrating?

I do a lot of backend and frontend web development, mainly on open source projects like Wordpress.

I’ve tried Windsurf and Cursor with Sonnet 3.5 and GPT-4o.

I find it incredibly frustrating for anything other basic boilerplating. It’s incredibly frequent that I spell out what I want as specifically as I can, and it makes massive unwanted changes to my code. It’s almost as if it’s saying “I don’t know why this is here (even if the code is perfectly functional), so I’ll just remove it”. Often times, these are breaking changes. [...] explained visually | DL5")

Both of these are really good. If you don’t know how neural networks work, he has some older videos that get into the basics of that.

I think most of these issues come from the fact that the model is working in isolation from the actual codebase.

If it only sees a prompt, it has no way to verify conventions, naming, or even whether `fooX` and `fooY` are used consistently: so it ends up guessing.

`fooX`
`fooY`

In my experience, once you connect it to the real workspace (files, search, history), a lot of these problems become much less severe. It still doesn’t “understand” in a human sense, but it stops being purely speculative.
